raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old boy, medically free, with history of unpasteurized milk ingestion, living in Shaqra (a village 200 km far from Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia), presented to our emergency department with fever, vomiting, and malaise for 2 weeks followed by 5-day history of left hypochondrial pain. He lost 9 kgs in the preceding two months. He had no history of trauma or surgery. He was admitted to a peripheral hospital where he received a course of antibiotics with no improvement. On clinical examination, he looked ill, in pain with a temperature of 38.4 degree Celsius; pulse rate of 116 beats per minutes; blood pressure 111/68 mmHg; and respiratory rate of 21 breaths per minute. Abdominal examination revealed moderate tenderness in the left hypochondrium, no organomegaly on palpation and normal bowel sounds.
 Laboratory investigation showed white blood cell count 4.12 x 109/L; hemoglobin 11.80 g/dL; platelet count 364 x 109/L; ESR 61 mm/H; CRP 66.5 mg/L; amylase 509 U/L; lipase 471 U/L; alanine transaminase 45 U/I; aspartate transaminase 32 U/I; alkaline phosphatase 162 U/I; gamma GT 86 U/I; total bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL; albumin 39 g/L; creatinine 0.5 mg/dL; urea 3.2 mmol/L; and lactate dehydrogenase, 303 U/I. Chest X-ray was normal. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. Abdominal X-ray showed no evidence of intestinal obstruction. Computed tomography of abdomen showed multiple irregular peripheral hypodense splenic lesions suggestive of splenic infarcts and borderline splenomegaly, with no evidence of acute pancreatitis and patent splenic veins with no thrombosis (Figure 1). Blood culture grew Brucella species after 88 hours of incubation. Brucella serology using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay was positive for IgM. Transesophageal echocardiography was negative. Lupus anticoagulant and anti-cardiolipin antibodies were negative. Proteins C and S were negative. JAK2 mutation was negative.
 Treatment of brucellosis with rifampicin 600 mg daily (for 6 weeks), doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (for 6 weeks), and gentamycin 300 mg daily (for 7 days) was given to him.
On the 8th day of admission, fever and abdominal pain resolved. High amylase and lipase were normalized and the patient was discharged home in good condition. After 3-month follow-up in outpatient clinic, the patient remained well with significant improvement of splenic infarcts on computed tomography (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of fever, vomiting, and malaise, followed by a 5-day history of left hypochondrial pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fever, vomiting, and malaise 2 weeks prior to presentation, followed by the onset of left hypochondrial pain 5 days prior. He had lost 9 kg over the preceding 2 months. He was initially admitted to a peripheral hospital and given a course of antibiotics without improvement before presenting to the emergency department.
subjective.past_medical_history: Medically free with no history of trauma or surgery. Residence: Shaqra village (200 km from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia). Epidemiological exposure: history of unpasteurized milk ingestion. Prior course of ineffective antibiotics at peripheral hospital.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, vomiting, malaise, left hypochondrial pain, 9 kg weight loss over 2 months. Home medications: prior ineffective antibiotic course (specific agents not documented). Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Appeared ill and in pain. Temperature: 38.4 °C; pulse rate: 116 beats/min; blood pressure: 111/68 mmHg; respiratory rate: 21 breaths/min. Abdomen: moderate tenderness in the left hypochondrium; no organomegaly palpated; normal bowel sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 4.12 x 10^9/L; Hemoglobin: 11.80 g/dL; Platelets: 364 x 10^9/L; ESR: 61 mm/h; CRP: 66.5 mg/L; Amylase: 509 U/L; Lipase: 471 U/L; ALT: 45 U/L; AST: 32 U/L; ALP: 162 U/L; GGT: 86 U/L; Total bilirubin: 0.2 mg/dL; Albumin: 39 g/L; Creatinine: 0.5 mg/dL; Urea: 3.2 mmol/L; LDH: 303 U/L. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray: normal. Abdominal X-ray: no evidence of intestinal obstruction.
objective.advanced_workup: Computed tomography (CT) of abdomen: multiple irregular peripheral hypodense splenic lesions suggestive of splenic infarcts and borderline splenomegaly, with no evidence of acute pancreatitis and patent splenic veins without thrombosis. Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE): negative for vegetations. Thrombophilia panel: Lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, protein C, protein S, and JAK2 mutation were all negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Systemic brucellosis complicated by multiple peripheral splenic infarcts, borderline splenomegaly, and secondary pancreatic enzyme elevation.
Confirmation: Blood culture grew Brucella species after 88 hours of incubation; Brucella serology by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was positive for IgM.
Differentials ruled out: Infective endocarditis (negative TEE); acute pancreatitis (normal pancreatic parenchyma on CT); hereditary or acquired thrombophilia/hypercoagulable state (negative antiphospholipid antibodies, protein C, protein S, and JAK2 mutation).
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with oral rifampicin (600 mg daily for 6 weeks), oral doxycycline (100 mg BID for 6 weeks), and parenteral gentamicin (300 mg daily for 7 days). On day 8 of admission, fever and abdominal pain resolved, elevated amylase and lipase normalized, and he was discharged home; at 3-month follow-up, he remained asymptomatic with significant CT improvement of splenic infarcts.
